This topic has be so torn. As a person that's working in IT, and made it all the way from "I barely know anything" to "I can design a network for an enterprise, cable it, test it, and program it" AI has been... very useful moving to a smaller company where I have more on my plate. There's been many times where I've been digging through troves of documentation, just to ask claude about my problem very naturally and get a very accurate response, as well as a conversational troubleshooting ability that lets me progress through complex problems step-by-step.... That's saved me HUNDREDS of hours in my life... At the same time.... some of these things I see AI doing now are the exact things I did to learn and achieve what I did now... and a lot of that prior knowledge is what allows me to assess/evaluate what these AIs give me as valid or not. There's AI network diagnostic tools for enterprise now, that basically replace the need for interns. A simple task like "Hey AP 12 says it's offline in the north dormitory for this college, can you go figure out why" would be something that a college IT team would likely give to that person trying to learn and grow. It's a perfect task for them. It's not critical, so they can take their time, and the issue could be any number of things so it's a true test of problem solving capabilities... but, with a tool like "Marvis" from juniper, as an admin I can simply ask it to diagnose this issue and it will examine the entire network stack from top to bottom and tell me exactly why it's failed. It'll tell me if there's a history of it failing. It is so good usually, that as a network admin, the role I use to sublet to a lower rung on the totem pole, to save time to be prioritized on other more important tasks, is now do-able by the computer itself. I have no need for the intern, and thus the intern becomes idle, and in the end, unnecessary as an expense to an organization. I think these, "entry" points to careers are at risk... The experts in fields will have their tasks augmented, but the roles that were there simply as time-savers for higher level roles, might be the ones most at risk.
